title: What breaks wudu
hookLine: using the toilet, deep sleep, passing wind, and details that differ by school

cards: A man from Hadramawt, in the south of Arabia, has heard Abu Hurayrah repeat a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: the prayer of someone in a state of hadath isn't accepted until he makes wudu. Hadath.
It's a technical word, and the man doesn't pretend to know it. So he asks, out loud: what is hadath? And Abu Hurayrah gives him a plain answer.
Passing wind. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the exchange, at number 135, question and answer together.

teach.h: WUDU LASTS UNTIL SOMETHING ENDS IT.
teach.b: Wudu isn't a once-a-day stamp. It lasts until something ends it, and the fiqh books call those things nawaqid, the breakers. The schools share a core.
Whatever leaves the body by the two private passages: using the toilet, passing wind.

teach.h: THE SHARED CORE: TOILET, WIND, DEEP SLEEP.
teach.b: Deep sleep, the kind where you lose track of yourself; a hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud, number 203, ties sleep to wudu. And losing consciousness.

teach.h: THE SCHOOLS DIFFER ON THE DETAILS.
teach.b: Then come the details, where the schools part ways and say so.
Touching the skin of someone of the opposite sex: the Shafi'i school counts it as a breaker, the Hanafi school does not, and the Maliki school looks at whether there was desire.
Bleeding from a wound breaks wudu for the Hanafis and not for the Shafi'is.

And in Sahih Muslim, number 360, someone asks the Prophet ﷺ whether to make wudu after eating camel meat, and he says yes; the Hanbali school takes that as a breaker, while other schools read it differently.

So each school has its own list. Then there's the rule that steadies the whole thing. In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 137, a man tells the Prophet ﷺ he sometimes imagines something has happened during prayer.
The answer: don't leave the prayer unless you hear a sound or notice a smell.
Scholars turned that into a principle: certainty isn't removed by doubt.
Wudu ends for a reason, not a worry. And when it ends, the answer is simple. Wash again.

how: Muslims renew wudu after using the toilet, passing wind, deep sleep or losing consciousness, and follow their school on the debated cases, such as touching the opposite sex, bleeding, or eating camel meat; a passing doubt does not break it.

o: the things that end wudu, like sleep or the toilet
doubts that come up in the middle of a prayer
the sins that make a person's prayer not count

games.q: what breaks wudu — tap the pairs.
p: leave only for a sound or a smell
a breaker in the Hanbali school

s: a doubt during prayer breaks wudu
Bukhari 137: don't leave unless you hear a sound or notice a smell.
the schools all agree on every breaker
they share a core and differ on details like touch, bleeding and camel meat.
deep sleep is among the things that break wudu
it's in the shared core, tied to a hadith in Abu Dawud 203.

games.q: you're halfway through the prayer and a thought creeps in: did something just happen? you're not sure. what does the hadith say?
o: stop and redo your wudu to be safe.
keep praying unless you hear a sound or notice a smell.
finish, then pray it all again.
games.why: in Bukhari 137 the Prophet says not to leave the prayer unless there's a sound or a smell. scholars drew a principle from it: certainty isn't removed by doubt.

practice: Pick one small worry you're carrying right now, the kind the mind invents: did I lock the door, did I say the wrong thing, did that count.
Ask it the question from the hadith: did you hear a sound, did you notice a smell, is anything here certain, or only a feeling?
If nothing is certain, set it down for now; and if you pray and follow a school, its list of breakers is worth knowing instead of guessing.

wordCard.voice: What breaks wudu. A shared core, the toilet, wind, deep sleep, details that differ by school, and a doubt that breaks nothing. Today's word.
